title: Boghach Khan, Son of Dirse Khan
author: Anonymous (Book of Dede Korkut), adapted by Lantern

source.name: Dede Korkut Kitabı, Dresden manuscript, 1st boy ("Dirse hân oglı bogac hân boyını beyân ider") — adapted into English by Lantern; plot taken from the Turkish Wikisource transcription of the Dresden manuscript text
source.license: Public domain (anonymous medieval source text); this English adaptation is by Lantern

summaryTr: Çocuğu olmayan Dirse Han'ın oğlu Boğaç, genç yaşta azgın bir boğayı yener ve adını Dede Korkut'tan alır. Ama babasının kıskanç kırk yiğidi, baba ile oğlu karşı karşıya getirmek için tehlikeli bir oyun kurar. Dede Korkut Kitabı'nın ilk boyunun sade bir İngilizce uyarlaması.
paragraphs: ## The Black Tent
Long ago, the Oghuz people lived on wide green plains. They lived in tents, and they had many horses and sheep. Their greatest leader was Bayindir Khan. He was the khan of khans.

Every year, Bayindir Khan gave a big feast. The lords of the Oghuz came from far away to eat at his table. But the khan had a hard rule. He put up three tents on the grass. The white tent was for the men who had a son. The red tent was for the men who had a daughter. The black tent was for the men who had no children. These men had to sit on black felt and eat plain sheep stew. The khan said, "God is not kind to these men, and we will not be kind to them."

One year, a lord called Dirse Khan came to the feast. He was rich and brave, but he had no son and no daughter. The servants took him to the black tent. They put him on the black felt and brought him the stew.

Dirse Khan stood up. His face was red with anger. "What did I do?" he asked. "Did the khan not like my sword? Did he not like my table? Men with less than me sit in the white tent. Why must I sit here?"
"My lord, it is the khan's rule," the servants said. "We cannot change it."

Dirse Khan left the feast without eating. He rode home, angry and sad. When he saw his wife, he spoke to her in a hard voice. "We have no child," he said. "Is it your fault, or is it mine? Why does God not give us a son?"

His wife was a wise woman, and she did not answer in anger. "Please sit down," she said. "Anger will not give us a child. Get up and do something good. Put up your big tents. Kill horses, camels and sheep. Make a hill of meat and a lake of kumis, the milk drink of our people. Feed the hungry. Give clothes to the people who have none. Help the men who owe money. Then ask God for a son. Maybe the prayer of one good person will reach Him."
Dirse Khan was quiet for a while. Then he said, "You are right."

He did everything his wife said. He put up his big tents and killed many animals. There was meat like a hill and kumis like a lake. The hungry ate until they were full. The poor got new clothes. The men who owed money did not have to pay. Then all the guests lifted their hands and prayed for the khan to have a child.

God heard their prayer. Soon the khan's wife was going to have a baby. Some months later, she had a son. Dirse Khan was happier than ever before. He gave the baby to nurses, and they took good care of him.
## The Boy and the Bull
The boy grew fast. At fifteen, he was tall and strong, and he was not afraid of anything.

At that time, Dirse Khan often visited the camp of Bayindir Khan. The great khan had a terrible bull. It was so strong that it could break a rock into dust with its horns. Every summer and every autumn, the bull fought with a big male camel. The lords of the Oghuz sat together and watched, and Bayindir Khan watched with them.

One summer day, the servants brought the bull out. Three men held it on the right side, and three men held it on the left. They had strong iron chains. In the middle of the field, they let the bull go.

Some boys were playing with little bones near the field. Dirse Khan's son was playing with three servant boys. "Run!" the people shouted. "The bull is free!" The three servant boys ran away. But Dirse Khan's son did not run. He stood in the middle of the field and looked at the bull.

The bull ran at him. The boy hit it on the forehead with his fist. The bull moved back, and then it came again. The boy hit it again, harder. For a long time, the boy and the bull pushed against each other. Neither of them was winning.

Then the boy thought, "A builder puts a post under a roof to hold it up. I am like a post for this bull's head. Why must I be its post?" He pulled back his fist and stepped to the side. The bull had nothing to push against. It lost its balance and fell on its head. The boy took out his knife and ended the fight.
The lords of the Oghuz ran to the boy. "Well done!" they shouted. "This boy needs a name. Let Dede Korkut come. Let him give the name, and let the boy ask his father for a place of his own."
Dede Korkut was the wisest man of the Oghuz. He was a singer, a poet and a teller of tales. People believed that his words always came true. He took the boy by the hand and led him to Dirse Khan.

"Dirse Khan," said Dede Korkut, "give this boy a throne and a land to rule. Give him a fast horse to ride. Give him ten thousand sheep for meat. Give him a red camel to carry his things. Give him a tent with a golden top for shade. Give him a fine coat to wear."

Then he turned to the boy. "You fought a bull in front of Bayindir Khan," he said. "So your name will be Boghach. In our old language, boga means bull. I have given you your name, and may God give you a long life."
Dirse Khan was proud. He gave his son everything that Dede Korkut asked for. The boy sat on his own throne, and from that day everyone called him Boghach.
## The Forty Companions

Dirse Khan had forty companions. They were the men who always rode with him and ate at his table. Now Boghach was a young lord, and he was busy with his own life. He did not often think about his father's forty men, and they did not like it. They became jealous.
"Now the son is the important man," they said to each other. "Soon nobody will listen to us. We must turn the father against his son."

Twenty of them went to Dirse Khan. "My lord, we have bad news," they said. "Your son has gone mad. He took forty riders, and he goes all over the land of the Oghuz on his horse. He takes what he wants. He says rude things to old men. Bayindir Khan will hear about it, and he will be angry with you. It is better to have no son than a son like this. Kill him."
Dirse Khan was very angry. "Go and bring him here," he said. "I do not want a son like this. I will kill him."
Then the other twenty came and told the same lies, and they said even more. "Your son is stronger than you now, my lord," they said. "He is going to take your place."
Dirse Khan believed them. He did not ask his son one question.
"Your son will not come when we call him," the forty said. "He does not listen to us. So you must take him hunting. Take him into the hills, and finish it there."

The next morning, Dirse Khan took his son and the forty men to the hills. They went hunting for deer. Some of the forty rode to the boy and said, "Your father wants to see you ride. Chase the deer toward him. Let him see how fast your horse is and how well you shoot."
The boy was happy. "My father is going to be proud of me," he thought.
Other men went to Dirse Khan and whispered in his ear. "My lord, look. Your son is chasing the deer straight at you. When he shoots at a deer, he will shoot you. Kill him before he kills you."

Dirse Khan was afraid, and his heart was hard. He took his strong bow and pulled it back. The arrow flew, and it hit his son between the shoulders. The boy fell from his horse, and his blood ran on the ground.
Dirse Khan wanted to run to his son. But the forty did not let him. They took his horse by the reins and turned it round. They rode back to the camp, and they left the boy on the ground.
## The Mountain Flower

At the camp, the khan's wife was waiting. "Today is my son's first great hunt," she said happily. She had many animals killed for a feast. She put on her best clothes, took forty young women with her, and went out to meet her husband.
She looked at Dirse Khan's face. She looked to his right, and she looked to his left. She did not see her son. Her heart shook.
"Where is my son?" she asked. "You went out with him, and you came back alone. Where is the boy I waited for so long?"
Dirse Khan did not answer. The forty men said, "Do not be afraid, lady. Your son is safe. He is still hunting, and he will come home soon. The khan is tired and cannot talk now."

But the mother knew they were lying. She got on her horse, took her forty young women and rode to the hills. She came to Kazilik Mountain, where the snow stays all year. She searched and called her son's name. Then she saw crows and ravens flying down into a valley, and she rode that way.
The boy was lying on the ground. The birds smelled blood, and they wanted to come down to him. But he had two dogs, and they stayed close and chased the birds away.

While the boy was lying there, a man on a grey horse came to him. It was Khidr, the holy helper of people in trouble. He touched the wound three times with his hand. "Do not be afraid, my boy," he said. "You will not die from this. The flower of the mountain, with your mother's milk, will be your medicine." Then he was gone.

Soon the mother arrived. She saw her son lying in his blood, and she cried out in grief. "Open your eyes, my son! Say one word to me!" She was so sad that she began to curse the mountain. "May your rivers stop running! May your deer never run again!"

The boy heard her voice. He opened his eyes and looked at his mother's face. "Mother, please do not curse the mountain," he said. "It has done nothing wrong. The rivers and the deer have done nothing wrong. This came from my father's hand. And do not cry. I will not die from this wound. A holy man on a grey horse came to me. He said that the mountain flower and your milk are the medicine."

The young women picked mountain flowers. The mother tried to give her milk, but the first time, nothing came. The second time, nothing came. The third time, the milk came at last. They put the flowers and the milk on the wound. Then they lifted the boy onto a horse and took him home in secret. They gave him to the doctors, and they hid him from Dirse Khan.
In forty days, the wound was healed. The boy could ride and hold a sword again. But Dirse Khan did not know. He thought his son was dead.

The forty companions heard that the boy was alive, and they were afraid. "If Dirse Khan sees his son, he will learn the truth," they said. "Then he will punish us all." So they did not wait. They took Dirse Khan and tied his hands behind his back with a rope of hair. They put a rope around his neck, hit him, and led him away toward the land of the enemy. Dirse Khan was now a prisoner.
## Boghach Comes Home
Nobody in the camp knew that the khan was a prisoner. But his wife heard the news, and she ran to her son.

"Do you know what has happened?" she said. "The forty men have taken your father. They tied his hands and took him to the enemy. Get up, my son. Take forty young riders and save your father. Your father hurt you, but you must not hurt him."
Boghach did not say one angry word. He stood up and put his sword on his belt. He took his bow and got on his horse. He called forty young riders, and they rode after his father's trail.

The forty traitors had stopped to rest. They were drinking and laughing. Then they saw a rider coming fast. "Look, a young man is coming," they said. "Let's catch him and send him to the enemy with the khan."

Dirse Khan was sitting on the ground with his hands tied. He did not know that the rider was his son. "My friends," he said, "I beg you. Free my hands and give me my kopuz, my old instrument with strings. I will speak to that young man and turn him back. After that, you can kill me or keep me alive."

The forty untied his hands and gave him his kopuz. He walked toward the rider and sang a song. "Young man, turn back. If you want my horses, my sheep, my camels or my tents, I will give them to you without a fight. If you came to save me, there is no need. I killed my own son. You have done nothing wrong. Go back."
The rider answered with a song, too. "Old man, I have horses and sheep and tents of my own. I do not want yours. But I will not leave my old father with the white beard to these forty traitors."

Then he gave a sign, and his forty young riders rushed forward. Boghach fought bravely. He fought the forty traitors and beat them. Some of them died in the fight, and he took the others prisoner. Then he freed his father.
Dirse Khan looked at the young man's face, and at last he knew. His son was alive! His son had come to save him. The boy he had hurt had saved him.

Now the khan understood everything. The forty had lied to him from the first day. They wanted power, but they lost everything. The man they had hurt was free again, and the boy they had lied about was a hero.
Bayindir Khan, the khan of khans, heard the whole story. He gave Boghach a throne and a land to rule.

Dede Korkut came and sang for them. "All people come into this world and go out of it," he sang. "Like a caravan, they stop for a night and move on. Death takes them all. But the stories stay. May your tall mountains never fall. May your shady trees never be cut. May your rivers never dry. May your white horse never trip. May your sword never break. And may God never make you need a bad man."

glossary.khidr: Hızır (zor durumdakilere yardıma gelen kutsal kişi)
glossary.may: (dilek) -sın / -sin (May your rivers never dry = Nehirlerin hiç kurumasın)

quiz.q: Which men had to sit in the black tent at Bayindir Khan's feast?
options: Men with a son
Men with a daughter
Men with no children
Men with no horses
quiz.explainTr: Beyaz çadır oğlu olanlar, kırmızı çadır kızı olanlar içindi; çocuğu olmayanlar kara çadıra oturtulurdu. Dirse Han da bu yüzden kara çadıra konur.

quiz.q: How did the boy win the fight with the bull?
options: He ran away and hid
He stepped to the side, and the bull fell
He used a long spear
His father helped him
quiz.explainTr: Çocuk yumruğunu çekip yana çekilir; boğa dayanacak bir şey bulamaz, dengesini kaybedip düşer. Sonra çocuk bıçağıyla işi bitirir.

quiz.q: Who gave the boy the name Boghach, and what does it come from?
options: His mother; it comes from the word for flower
Bayindir Khan; it comes from the word for mountain
His father; it comes from the word for hunter
Dede Korkut; it comes from the word for bull
quiz.explainTr: Adı Dede Korkut verir. "Boğa" sözünden gelen Boğaç, boğayı yenen çocuk için çok uygun bir addır.

quiz.q: Why did the forty companions tell lies about Boghach?
options: They were jealous and wanted power
They wanted to help Dirse Khan
They were afraid of the bull
Bayindir Khan told them to
quiz.explainTr: Kırk yiğit, Boğaç önem kazanınca nüfuzlarını kaybetmekten korkar ve kıskanır; bu yüzden baba ile oğlunu birbirine düşürmeye çalışırlar.

quiz.q: What did Boghach do at the end of the story?
options: He left the Oghuz lands forever
He asked Bayindir Khan to punish his father
He freed his father and beat the forty traitors
He gave his throne to the forty companions
quiz.explainTr: Annesinin sözüyle kırk genç atlıyla babasının peşinden gider, hainleri yener ve babasını kurtarır. Sonunda Bayındır Han ona taht verir.
